title: A Chief of Staff Who ‘Will Crack Skulls’
summary: In the days before MAGA’s midterm disaster, President Trump began complaining about his presidency. He felt stuck. The war in Iran wouldn’t end. Inflation wouldn’t subside. Little was going his way. But in the president’s mind, there was one exception: “Stephen is the only one who gets stuff done,” ...
content:
In the days before MAGA’s midterm disaster, President Trump began complaining about his presidency. He felt stuck. The war in Iran wouldn’t end. Inflation wouldn’t subside. Little was going his way. But in the president’s mind, there was one exception: “Stephen is the only one who gets stuff done,” Trump repeatedly griped, a person close to the White House told us. “I need more people who get stuff done.”

Stephen Miller, one of the president’s hardest-charging and longest-serving aides, had managed to maintain Trump’s trust, even though he is the architect of the administration’s sweeping mass-deportation campaign that many in the GOP blame, in part, for the Republicans’ historic wipeout this week. Today, Trump announced that Miller would replace Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, completing his decade-long journey from congressional staffer to the most powerful aide in Washington.

Where Wiles served as something of a guardrail—making sure Trump was fully briefed and that he understood the risks and pitfalls of any decision—Miller has played the role of an accelerant for a president who already has rash tendencies. One issue on which Wiles and Miller seem to diverge: how to force journalists to reveal their sources in the government. Trump has pushed the Department of Justice to pursue criminal-leak investigations on national-security grounds, and there have been discussions in the White House and at DOJ about various tactics they could use—including arrests—as part of those efforts, according to three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said that Wiles had pushed back. Miller, though, was in favor and insisted that it wouldn’t take long for journalists to give up their sources, they told us. A DOJ spokesperson told us via text that “this is absolutely false” but declined to elaborate. A White House spokesperson told us in a statement that unauthorized leaks will “NEVER be tolerated” and those responsible “must be held accountable.”

One person familiar with Trump’s decision to elevate Miller told us that the president wants somebody who “will crack skulls,” adding that Trump “doesn’t want to be reined in.” Another described Miller as someone with significant Capitol Hill experience who could manage the coming clashes with Democrats. White House officials have held high-level conversations in recent days, including with Miller, about areas where they can work with Democrats. But another person familiar with Trump’s thinking said there was no need for a chief of staff who could work the Hill to pass legislation, because nothing was going to get done. “The next two years are going to be nonstop political warfare,” this person told us—and Miller can be the face of that fight.

This account of Wiles’s ouster and Miller’s ascent is based on interviews with six people familiar with the situation, all of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. Inside the White House, officials understood that Trump would never blame himself for Republican midterm losses, and the West Wing has spent the past few days wondering whom Trump would punish. When The New York Times published a story about the defeat—with verbatim leaks of Trump’s top political team joking ahead of the election about how grim it all looked—Wiles found herself taking heat from the president. Two people familiar with the matter told us that Trump felt that the story, which featured Wiles’s allies seeming to laugh at Republican failure, was a betrayal, and he expressed his displeasure to her.

Trump met with Wiles on Wednesday, and she volunteered to resign, but no decision was made. By yesterday, Wiles was telling her deputies that she had a resignation letter ready and was prepared to leave. She had spent months running the White House while undergoing treatment for breast cancer, and has described herself as “tired” to colleagues. The president announced her departure today after the Times reached out to the White House about her rumored exit. Wiles did not view her role as a roadblock to Trump’s most extreme impulses. On many of the White House’s most consequential decisions, she did not directly weigh in. During the debate over the Iran war, for instance, advisers said, she focused on making sure that Trump was fully briefed on the risks, although others in the White House described her as concerned.

Her replacement, who takes over on Monday, is known both for his effectiveness and his hard-line views. Miller appeared with Trump tonight at an event at Mar-a-Lago and said: “I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

Miller has been with Trump from the beginning. He was an aide to Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who became the first senator to endorse Trump’s 2016 campaign. Before long, Miller was designing policy proposals—particularly those that reflected his hard-line immigration views—and sometimes appearing as a fiery warm-up act at Trump’s rallies. He co-authored the first term’s so-called Muslim ban, became known for his high-volume and belligerent TV interviews defending Trump, and was one of the few staffers to navigate the often-competing power centers in the dysfunctional West Wing. (In both terms, he has remained well liked by colleagues, who appreciate his straightforwardness and dry sense of humor.) Miller oversaw the writing of the speech that Trump delivered from the Ellipse on January 6, 2021, ahead of the Capitol insurrection, and his influence only grew during Trump’s four years out of power. Miller used that time to help write Project 2025, a playbook for Trump’s return to the White House that included a broad expansion of executive power.

At the core of Miller’s agenda was a sweeping deportation program. Masked ICE agents detained people in quiet neighborhoods and Home Depot parking lots, while Miller demanded that dramatic deportation quotas be met. Americans, polling showed, began to view the tactics as extreme, particularly after the killing of two Americans in Minneapolis early this year. Trump’s political team has privately blamed Miller’s aggressive immigration policy in part for the defeat on Tuesday, because violent ICE clashes and ethnic profiling on the streets have alienated both Latino voters and moderate independents.

Miller has already been operating as a de facto chief of staff for the Department of Homeland Security and the president’s mass-deportation campaign. He hosts conference calls six days a week with top officials from agencies across the government who are enlisted to help ICE with the crackdown. Officials who participate in the calls say that Miller often berates staff who disappoint him or lack the information he wants. The White House press office promised in a statement tonight that Miller “will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.”

[Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide]

Recently, Trump had begun telling people close to him that he was considering changing his immigration emphasis, recognizing that although voters supported his tough border-security stance, ICE’s brutal approach to rounding up undocumented immigrants, including those who are not criminals, was provoking a backlash. Trump had begun to hear from business owners about their employees being deported, along with the nannies and tutors of friends, and he was open to pivoting. Miller, as his chief of staff, will now directly oversee the policy debate, a shift from his role as the resident immigration hawk in the White House.  

Since 2021, Wiles has been responsible for building the political campaign—and, later, the White House structure—around Trump. After January 6, at a time when most Republicans were keeping their distance from Trump, she offered him a core group of advisers, bringing in the veteran campaign strategist Chris LaCivita to help run the 2024 campaign, along with the strategists Taylor Budowich and James Blair, operatives with Florida political experience who would go on to senior roles in the White House. (Miller during this period operated outside the president’s inner circle, from a new legal operation focused on pursuing MAGA priorities.) Inside the White House, she was known for her calm and organization, and her ability to do what no other chief of staff to Trump had ever done: Guide the sometimes-mercurial president, regularly stepping in to try to prevent risky decisions, while at the same time allowing him to run his presidency on his own terms.

Wiles was well liked by many Republicans who appreciated the degree of levelheadedness she brought to the West Wing. She grew up as the daughter of an alcoholic, the football play-by-play caller Pat Summerall. Trump does not drink, but in an interview with Vanity Fair in 2025, Wiles said there were similarities between her father and the president, who she said had an “alcoholic’s personality,” and that had helped her in the job. But she slowed down this year. In March, shortly after the conflict with Iran began, she was diagnosed with breast cancer, forcing her to spend much of the campaign season juggling one of the most demanding jobs in government with regular chemotherapy appointments. She described the ordeal as “brutal and unrelenting,” and said that she sometimes had to fight to get out of bed. Trump’s poll numbers collapsed, largely because of high prices fueled by the war and his haphazard tariffs program.

Wiles had built a team of loyalists—to both her and the president—in the White House and steered the West Wing to a series of successes last year, including passing its signature piece of legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. At the start of the term, White House advisers, including Wiles, took steps to turn the broad coalition that had elected Trump into regular Republican voters.

Wiles never stopped the president from relying on other advisers as well—both in and outside the administration. In recent weeks, some of those advisers became more crucial. Corey Lewandowski, who clashed with Wiles during the 2024 campaign, shared a social-media post after the election blaming Republican “political consultants” for giving “really bad advice.” And just hours before Trump announced Wiles’s departure, a former deputy to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Calley Means, appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast and accused the chief of staff of standing in the way of the Make America Healthy Again agenda by siding with pesticide, tobacco, and food-industry concerns during policy debates.

[Read: The White House’s MAHA gatekeeper]

Other powerful forces in Trump’s orbit also targeted Wiles. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte—who recently generated a minor scandal by spilling cola on the carpet of Trump’s new Air Force One, two people told us—had complained that she was holding Trump back. (Pulte has publicly praised Wiles.) And Miller’s wife, Katie, a former aide in the White House and to Elon Musk who is an influential voice in MAGA circles, began to push for her husband’s ascension. Stephen Miller, his supporters say, is the right person to steer the final two years of Trump’s presidency. Despite the scale of this week’s Democratic victory, the president has rarely reached across the aisle in the past. In recent days, he made his feelings known with a new red hat displayed on the Resolute Desk. It was emblazoned with a single word: VETO.

Nick Miroff contributed to this report.

title: A Preposterous, Overpriced, Beautiful Disaster of a Car
summary: The most important Cybertruck ever built is probably still parked somewhere on the grounds of Mar-a-Lago. In August 2024, Donald Trump stood on the driveway of his Palm Beach club and circled a custom version of Tesla’s notorious, angular electric truck. Wrapped in a giant photo of his bloodied face...
content:
The most important Cybertruck ever built is probably still parked somewhere on the grounds of Mar-a-Lago. In August 2024, Donald Trump stood on the driveway of his Palm Beach club and circled a custom version of Tesla’s notorious, angular electric truck. Wrapped in a giant photo of his bloodied face after the assassination attempt that summer, the car was a gift from the MAGA influencer Adin Ross during a livestreamed interview. “Wow, that’s an Elon!” Trump said.

When Trump returned to the presidency, Elon Musk’s truck became a defining symbol of his second term—a MAGA hat on wheels. Like the president himself, the Cybertruck is thought of differently by different people: brash, unsophisticated, or badass. And like the world’s richest man and former head of DOGE, the Cybertruck moves fast and breaks things with little regard for anything in its way. If nothing else, the Cybertruck is unique: Here is a car that is marketed as bulletproof and has a windshield wiper (only one wiper) that Musk has compared to a “katana.” Now the Cybertruck is about to be something else: discontinued. Early this morning, Musk announced on X that he will wind down production of the Cybertruck by the middle of next year to free up factory space to make Cybercabs, the robotaxis that Tesla is attempting to roll out across the country.

No matter how you feel about it, the Cybertruck will go down as a tremendous flop in Silicon Valley history. When the car was first released, in November 2023, Musk called it the “best product” that he’s ever released. As Musk bankrolled Trump’s 2024 presidential run and then joined him in Washington, MAGA supporters enthusiastically embraced the Cybertruck. Fast-forward to 2026, and almost no one wants to buy one. The shift has been telling: The midterms were disastrous for Musk, who blew nearly $500 million boosting unsuccessful Republican candidates, especially in Texas, where Tesla is based. Musk’s discontinuation of the Cybertruck may be seen, among other things, as political triage, a way of wiping his hands clean of a car that liberals have branded as the “Deplorean.”

[Read: My day inside America’s most hated car]

Still, it would be a mistake to remember the truck as nothing more than the apotheosis of two years of Trumpian (and Muskian) excess. The Cybertruck was a meme and a culture-war totem, but it was also just a car. And on that front, Musk’s creation was especially a letdown. When he first announced the car in 2019, it was a revelation, no matter how ugly: After proving that electric cars could be more than just souped-up golf carts, his car company would now bring EVs to the masses. The Cybertruck, Musk promised, would start at just $40,000, a fraction of the cost of Tesla’s other cars at the time. By the time the Cybertruck was actually for sale, it came with a sticker price of $100,000.

In some ways, the truck was doomed from the beginning: Building a vehicle that ignores the principles of basic aerodynamics isn’t exactly cheap or easy. Dogged by one problem after the next—stainless-steel panels that can fall off, a faulty accelerator pedal that can get stuck and turn the car into a cruise missile—the Cybertruck did not entice very many people to actually put up the money for one. Within a week of the vehicle’s unveiling, Musk said that 250,000 had preordered one. But in three years, he has sold a total of only 70,000 Cybertrucks.

In spite of all the problems, the Cybertruck actually is a pretty fun car. It’s difficult to maneuver and more than a little impractical. But you can’t take a Zoom call from the front seat of a Toyota Camry, or have that vehicle make fart noises when a passenger sits down. Musk’s creation was absurd, but it was different. Few other vehicles can say that.

America desperately needs what the Cybertruck could have been. Electric cars offer the possibility of redesigning vehicles from the ground up. In China, you can buy EVs with built-in fridges and headlights that can project movies. In the U.S., however, automakers have mostly just duped the gas cars we’re all familiar with. Even during this moment of high gas prices, Americans have been stubbornly unwilling to go electric. It’s hard not to wonder how many more electric cars would be on the streets if the Cybertruck had actually lived up to its original promise.

The Cybertruck was not the best product Musk ever made—not even close—but it’s the product that reveals the most about his motivations and impulses. It is a cautionary tale of Musk’s habit of overpromising and under-delivering. (Data centers in space! Robots that can water your plants!) Most of all, the Cybertruck is another reminder—in this case, a nearly 7,000-pound one—that the influence of the world’s richest man does have limits.

title: Harmeet Dhillon’s Tenure of Destruction
summary: Harmeet Dhillon is not the most notable administration official to depart after Democrats’ enormous midterm victory—that title goes to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who President Trump announced today would be replaced by Stephen Miller. But Dhillon’s short tenure shows the immense influen...
content:
Harmeet Dhillon is not the most notable administration official to depart after Democrats’ enormous midterm victory—that title goes to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who President Trump announced today would be replaced by Stephen Miller. But Dhillon’s short tenure shows the immense influence that Trump has had on the federal government in less than two years in power.

Her departure comes as Democrats prepare a long list of investigations they hope to pursue once they take control of the House and Senate in January. As results streamed in on Tuesday night, Robert Garcia, the incoming head of the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word statement to Trump appointees: “Lawyer up.” Jamie Raskin, the presumptive head of the Judiciary Committee, has promised intense scrutiny of the Justice Department. Having stepped down, Dhillon will have more time to spend with her lawyers ahead of the inevitable hearings.

Dhillon had reportedly been campaigning for a promotion to a higher position at DOJ, which was apparently not forthcoming. CBS News reports that Trump wanted her fired for remarks about the supposed crisis of voting by noncitizens in a recent 60 Minutes interview that he found insufficiently bellicose. But she can depart with the satisfaction of completing the task she set out to achieve: doing immense damage to the Civil Rights Division, long known as the “crown jewel” of the department. “We changed it, and that’s what we came here to do,” she told Fox News. “And it’s done.” She’s right.

Dhillon’s goal, my colleague Quinta Jurecic wrote in a definitive April profile, was to reshape the division in Trump’s name and turn its historic focus on protecting civil rights upside down. “She has used the branch’s resources to investigate school districts and colleges over DEI, back the White House’s push to gain Republican congressional seats through redistricting, and prosecute journalists covering an anti-ICE protest in Minnesota,” Quina wrote. The division also gave up on holding police departments accountable for civil-rights abuses, abandoning proposed agreements with departments in Minneapolis and Louisville, Kentucky, that resulted from investigations after the murders of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor.

But as the midterms drew closer, a major focus was elections. Under Dhillon, the division pursued debunked and baseless claims of election fraud in Fulton County, Georgia, during the 2020 election. After the Supreme Court effectively threw out Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act this spring, Dhillon leaped to push states to redraw maps in order to reduce minority voting power. She twisted states’ arms to hand over voter rolls, part of a futile attempt by the administration to find evidence of widespread voting by noncitizens.

This pressure continued right up to Election Day. In the closing weeks of the campaign, the Justice Department tried to intimidate local and state election officials in states including California, Washington, and Alaska—aiming to put a thumb on the scales in service of Republican candidates. As the Cato Institute’s Walter Olson writes, the Trump administration failed to subvert the election, but not because it didn’t try.

When a president of a different party takes over the Justice Department, priorities naturally change. But some changes go beyond those normal shifts of emphasis. During the George W. Bush administration, an inspector general’s report described sweeping and improper politicization. In that instance, some 70 percent of attorneys left the division between 2003 and 2007. By comparison, as much as 80 percent of the division’s staff have left in the less than two years of the Trump presidency.

Dhillon’s Civil Right Division did have some notable failures. For example, the attempt to acquire voter rolls was a flop. The administration suffered an astonishing string of 27 losses in federal district courts in related cases, and drew harsh criticism even from Republican state officials. As one last indignity, lawyers from the Civil Rights Division failed to obtain an indictment from a grand jury for Cassidy Hutchinson, a former Trump aide who testified to the House January 6 Committee. Outside observers noted that bringing civil-rights charges against Hutchinson, rather than simply charging her with false statements, was a peculiar choice.

In sum, Dhillon leaves the Civil Rights Division in terrible shape: Its ranks are depleted, its work is interrupted, and its credibility with juries and judges is in tatters. Justice Connection, an advocacy group for former DOJ employees, issued a statement decrying her tenure. “After she upended the division’s mission-critical work, the civil servants who dedicated their careers to protecting vulnerable communities were instead told to target them—and more than three-quarters of the division’s lawyers left,” Stacey Young, its executive director, said. “For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it.”

Dhillon might have been able to boil the same sentiment down to just two words: Mission accomplished.

title: A Monster of His Time
summary: The criminal trial of Russell Brand took less than four weeks, at the end of which the comedian turned spiritual influencer was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (The jury in London declared him not guilty of three other charges, two of rape and one of attempted i...
content:
The criminal trial of Russell Brand took less than four weeks, at the end of which the comedian turned spiritual influencer was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (The jury in London declared him not guilty of three other charges, two of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.) The accounts detailed by Brand’s accusers were harrowing. The Christianity-themed podcast episodes broadcast by Brand and his wife, Laura, before and during the trial—their regular series is titled Sunday Service With the Brands—were so audacious that they were hard to process. In one installment, Brand interrupted his own monologue on how a Bible passage from Ephesians helped him prepare for court each day (“Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled round your waist”) so that he could read a sponsored ad for Polymarket.

Still, what shocked me most during the trial was how many of the women detailed assaults that they said happened to them while they were at work. One complainant testified that while she was employed at MTV in 2001, Brand had tried to drag her into the office bathroom for sex, becoming a “wild-eyed maniac,” in her words. (Brand was found not guilty on this charge.) Another complainant stated that Brand had squeezed her breasts and kissed her in broad view of his entourage while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in the mid-2000s, a charge on which he was convicted. A woman working for the British national TV broadcaster Channel 4 in 2009 testified that Brand had refused to film one day unless she gave him a massage, and when she’d acquiesced, he’d buried his face in her crotch while two of his associates watched and laughed. (Brand was also found guilty of this charge.)

In court, Brand’s accusers were asked whether they’d told anyone else what had happened to them at the time (yes, they had told colleagues, two out of three of the above women said), and what had happened in response (nothing). The line of questioning was perhaps necessary in a court of law but seemed ironic given that Brand’s entire career throughout the 2000s was built on transgressions very like the ones detailed in court, broadcast as national entertainment.

[Read: The unspeakable, enabled]

It’s easy to forget, deep into Brand’s third and fourth professional reincarnations as an online conspiracy theorist and an evangelist, that he became famous for relentless provocation. His persona—a mix of lolloping Dickensian scoundrel, glam-rock dandy, and grinning sexual deviant—was unique when he broke out as a comic in 2000. In a moment when the cheerful sexism of 1990s British culture was edging toward a darker mode, Brand’s willingness to violate every moral and social code was the core of his identity.

In 2001, the day after 9/11, he was fired by MTV after showing up to work dressed as Osama bin Laden, with his own drug dealer in tow. In 2002, he filmed scenes for his satellite-TV show, Re:Brand, during which he took baths with an unhoused person and masturbated a man in a pub bathroom. (In his defense, he later specified, he was on crack and heroin at the time.) That year, Brand was also fired from his XFM radio show for reading pornographic material on the air. But every time he lost a job, he gained a better and more prestigious one.

One woman testified in court that at a party in Soho in 2004—the same year that Brand was hired for his most high-profile gig yet, as the host of a show spun off from the smash reality series Big Brother—he’d grabbed her breasts and forced his penis into her mouth (he was convicted of only the former act). In 2006, the same year that he began hosting a BBC Radio Six show, Brand asked the TV presenter Vanessa Feltz, on another of his shows, whether he could “have it off” with her daughters, and harassed the singer Dannii Minogue so committedly that she described him as a “vile predator” who “wouldn’t take no for an answer.”

All of this—the ritualistic diminishment of women doing their jobs, the ironic cruelty, the swaggering priapism—was so much a part of Brand’s schtick that it must have been what producers and commissioners liked about him. British culture was deeply confused about sex at the time: The waning anxiety of the AIDS era and the nascent force of the internet meant that sexual imagery was suddenly everywhere, and no one seemed to know the rules anymore. As a teenager in 1999, just home from school, I watched the pop stars Geri Halliwell and Kylie Minogue arm-wrestle and then make out on camera for the Channel 4 series TFI Friday, while the host, Chris Evans, cheered them on and replayed the footage, eyes darting out of his head like a cartoon coyote. In 2008, the BBC TV presenter Jonathan Ross simply told Gwyneth Paltrow on his talk show that he “would fuck her.”

Brand could only have emerged in this postfeminist moment, when people were still sanguine about objectifying women for sport, and not yet jaded by the extremities of the internet. What do people commonly do when they’re shocked? They laugh. Brand’s body of comedic work is made up of so many offenses, detailed by Brand himself in baroque and head-spinning verbiage, that to try to take stock of them all now feels like trying to compile the dictionary. In his 2007 memoir, My Booky Wook (supposedly titled after the Nadsat dialect spoken by the rapist marauders in A Clockwork Orange), Brand describes, during high school, badgering a teenage girl named Penny for sex: “I painted verbal pictures and begged until she kissed me, I lied and danced and evoked the spirit of Pan till reluctantly she removed her bra, I used tears and emotional blackmail to secure the immolation of her knickers.”

[Read: No, women aren’t the problem]

Early in the days of his BBC radio show, Brand called a female newscaster “erotic,” saying, “We’re going to get under that desk and we’re gonna unleash hell on your thighs, woman.” (The woman complained to colleagues, causing Brand to further mock her on the air. “The producer just told me that we’ve upset her,” he said on another show. “They go, ‘She ain’t got the right to reply.’”) To Piers Morgan, in a 2006 GQ interview, Brand said that although he’d likely slept with close to 2,000 women, “I resent the word ‘predator.’ I like to think of myself as a conduit of natural forces. After all, the most natural thing in the world for people to do is f*, isn’t it? And people want to do it, so all you have to do is remove all the reasons why women don’t actually go through with it.”

Brand’s defense lawyers, and his own testimony in court, maintained throughout that although he’d been an admitted—and eventually repentant—philanderer during the height of his fame, he had never had sex with a woman without her consent. The jury disagreed. The judge said yesterday that Brand will likely face “significant” time in prison, given the gravity of the offenses of which he was found guilty.

It’s notable that in the years following 2010, as Brand’s acting roles puttered out and rumors circulated about what he was like to work with, he had to constantly reinvent himself to try to keep people’s attention. But his role at the beginning of the 21st century as the glinty-eyed, chaotic, intensely self-obsessed purveyor of sexual discomfort made him a mascot for his era, and he was enabled by far more people than will ever admit to it. “There was a culture of fear,” one of the complainants said in court about Channel 4, her workplace when Brand assaulted her. “Russell Brand was an A-lister star, it was Big Brother, people were watching it, we all watched it.”

title: Trump Doubles Down With Miller
summary: Introspection has never been one of Donald Trump’s more notable attributes. He never accepts blame or course-corrects; he only becomes a more distilled version of himself.And so, faced with rejection at the ballot box on an overwhelming scale, the president responded by replacing his chief of staff,...
content:
Introspection has never been one of Donald Trump’s more notable attributes. He never accepts blame or course-corrects; he only becomes a more distilled version of himself.

And so, faced with rejection at the ballot box on an overwhelming scale, the president responded by replacing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller.

Technically speaking, Miller had been Wiles’s second in command, as deputy chief of staff. In reality, Miller was already the administration’s most powerful figure, arguably including Trump himself. Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser and a Miller ally who was briefly cast as the power behind the throne during Trump’s first term, described Miller earlier this year as Trump’s “prime minister.” In a parliamentary system, the president or monarch is merely the symbolic head of state, whereas the prime minister is the head of government.

Wiles, though reputed for her professionalism and competence, held her job for nearly two years by facilitating Trump’s impulses without questioning them. Miller, however, has driven and shaped those impulses.

He is fanatically post-liberal. Miller has repeatedly described the opposition as illegitimate. “The Democrat Party is not a political party,” he said last year. “It is a domestic extremist organization.” He has obsessively, and effectively, employed executive actions to circumvent Congress as a lawmaking body. Trump had little use for the legislature even when his allies controlled it. If Miller remains true to form, he will extend his reliance on executive action, and commit the administration to total defiance of any oversight.

He is especially driven by his belief that immigration is a plot directed by left-wing elites to destroy traditional America. Miller, more than any other single factor, explains Trump’s baffling choice to blow up his 2024 coalition, which registered shocking gains among Latinos. He has directed the administration’s frantic campaign of mass deportation, acting in the belief that the GOP has four years to permanently reshape American demography or face permanent extinction. Miller, more than any other person, is responsible for unleashing violent havoc on American streets, as masked agents in unmarked vehicles have swept up suspects. He has also virtually shut down legal immigration—except for white South Africans, whom the administration has ostentatiously welcomed. Even Trump, according to The Wall Street Journal, has sometimes complained that Miller’s immigration enforcement has gone too far.

Miller’s enforcement regimen is obviously not the sole cause of Trump’s unpopularity. Trump’s tariffs, corruption, cuts to health care, obsession with erecting monuments to or renaming them for himself, and the war with Iran all contributed to the disintegration of his coalition. When J. D. Vance laid all of the blame on the war, absolving every other failure, it sent a signal that the administration would tolerate criticism only in this one, single realm.

The signal sent by Miller’s elevation takes that message to the next step. Miller pitched himself to Trump as an advocate of winding down the war with Iran, The New York Times’ Maggie Haberman reported. His elevation thus combines retreat on a single front—a front many Trump devotees regard as a betrayal of his “America First” principles—with a determination to advance on every other.

Trump dwells in a zero-sum world, divided between winners and losers. His instinct in a moment of defeat is to empower an aide who he himself recognizes has at times gone too far. But Trump cannot admit he has failed, or bring himself to show any weakness. Better to go too far than not far enough.

title: U.S. Attorney Who Oversaw Centerpiece of Trump’s Revenge Campaign Resigns
summary: The Southern District of Florida had more than 200 lawyers when Jason A. Reding Quiñones arrived, but by the fall it fell to slightly more than half that number, after a spate of firings and resignations.

title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
summary: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their familiesThe leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters i...
content:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
summary: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 resultThe African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally wi...
content:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

content:
Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit

A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
summary: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cutsThe African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crum...
content:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.

title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg

content:
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective

Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
